reference_title: Ground Modification Methods Reference Manual – Volume I

sections.title: Deep Dynamic Compaction (DDC) - Description
sections.summary: Deep dynamic compaction (DDC) densifies loose granular soils and partially saturated fills by repeatedly dropping heavy tampers (5-40 tonnes) from heights of 10-40 m using cranes. Developed by Menard in France in the 1960s. Applied in grids with tamper prints at 2-5 m spacing; multiple passes at decreasing energy (high energy for depth, ironing pass for surface). Not effective in saturated fine-grained soils.
sections.body: Deep dynamic compaction (DDC) is a ground improvement technique that densifies loose granular soils and partially saturated cohesive fills by repeatedly dropping heavy weights from significant heights onto the ground surface. Developed by Louis Menard in France in the 1960s, the technique uses steel or concrete tamper weights of 5 to 40 tonnes dropped from heights of 10 to 40 m using conventional crawler cranes or specialty rigs. The impact energy is transmitted as stress waves that propagate through the soil mass, causing particle rearrangement in granular soils and collapse of metastable structures in collapsible fills. DDC treatment typically involves multiple passes: a high-energy pass on a wide grid (6-12 m centers) to treat deep layers, followed by a low-energy ironing pass on a closer grid to treat shallow material. The ground surface experiences craters 0.3 to 2.0 m deep after each impact, which are backfilled with granular material between passes. DDC is one of the most cost-effective ground improvement methods for large treatment areas in granular soils.
key_points: Densifies loose granular soils and partially saturated cohesive fills by dropping heavy weights from height
Developed by Louis Menard in France in the 1960s
Tamper weights: 5-40 tonnes; drop heights: 10-40 m; uses crawler cranes or specialty rigs
Impact energy transmitted as stress waves causing particle rearrangement and collapse of metastable structures
Multiple passes: high-energy deep pass (6-12 m grid), low-energy ironing pass (closer grid)
Ground craters 0.3-2.0 m deep after each impact; backfilled between passes
Most cost-effective ground improvement for large treatment areas in granular soils

sections.title: DDC Feasibility
sections.summary: DDC is most effective in freely draining granular soils with <15% fines. Effectiveness decreases significantly above 15% fines; not recommended for saturated clays or silts. DDC can treat loose fills, collapsible soils, sinkholes, and karst. Vibration monitoring required near existing structures; typical exclusion zone 20-50 m from sensitive structures.
sections.body: DDC is most effective in freely draining granular soils (sands and gravels) with less than 15% fines content, where excess pore water pressures generated by impact dissipate rapidly between drops. Effectiveness decreases significantly as fines content increases above 15%, and DDC is generally not recommended for saturated clays or silts where pore pressures cannot dissipate between drops. DDC has also been successfully applied to collapsible soils (loess, compacted fills placed dry of optimum), municipal solid waste, and mine spoils. Site access must accommodate heavy cranes (typically 50-150 tonne capacity), and a minimum buffer distance of 30-60 m from existing structures is required to limit ground vibrations and lateral soil displacements. Vibrations from DDC typically generate peak particle velocities (PPV) of 10-50 mm/s at a distance equal to the treatment depth, attenuating approximately proportional to 1/sqrt(r) with distance r. Pre-construction survey of surrounding structures and vibration monitoring during construction are essential.
key_points: Most effective in granular soils with fines content < 15%
Not recommended for saturated clays or silts where pore pressures cannot dissipate
Also effective for collapsible soils (loess), municipal solid waste, and mine spoils
Requires heavy cranes (50-150 tonne capacity) and 30-60 m buffer from existing structures
Vibrations: PPV of 10-50 mm/s at distance equal to treatment depth
Vibration attenuation approximately proportional to 1/sqrt(r)
Pre-construction survey and vibration monitoring are essential
equations: PPV \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{r}}, approximate vibration attenuation with distance r from impact
sections.applicability: Feasibility screening for DDC based on soil type, fines content, groundwater, and proximity to existing structures.

sections.title: DDC Depth of Influence
sections.summary: Maximum depth of improvement: D = n × sqrt(W × H), where D = depth (m), W = tamper weight (tonnes), H = drop height (m), n = empirical coefficient (0.3-0.8, typically 0.5 for initial estimates). The equation is empirical and should be calibrated to site conditions. Effective treatment zone is typically 0.5 to 0.7 × D_max. Table 4-1 provides n values by soil type.
sections.body: The maximum depth of improvement from DDC is estimated using the empirical relationship D = n * sqrt(W * H), where D is the depth of influence in meters, W is the tamper weight in tonnes, H is the drop height in meters, and n is an empirical coefficient that depends on soil type and degree of saturation. The coefficient n typically ranges from 0.3 to 0.8 for most applications: n = 0.5 is commonly used as a conservative first estimate for granular soils, while values of 0.5-0.7 are typical for sands and gravels, and 0.3-0.4 for soils with significant fines content or partial saturation. Menard originally proposed n = 1.0, but field experience has shown that lower values are more appropriate for design. For a typical DDC operation with W = 15 tonnes and H = 20 m (applied energy = W*H = 300 tonne-m), the estimated depth of influence with n = 0.5 is D = 0.5 * sqrt(300) = 8.7 m. The depth of significant improvement is typically 2/3 to 3/4 of the theoretical depth D. Energy per unit area (applied energy divided by grid area) is the key parameter controlling the degree of improvement, with typical values of 150-300 kJ/m^2 for loose sands and 250-600 kJ/m^2 for collapsible soils.
key_points: Depth of influence: D = n * sqrt(W * H), fundamental DDC design equation
W = tamper weight (tonnes), H = drop height (m), n = empirical coefficient (0.3-0.8)
n = 0.5 is conservative first estimate for granular soils; n = 0.5-0.7 for sands/gravels
n = 0.3-0.4 for soils with significant fines or partial saturation

Energy per unit area: 150-300 kJ/m^2 for loose sands, 250-600 kJ/m^2 for collapsible soils

Eq 4-2: E_{applied} = W \cdot H, applied energy per drop (tonne-m or kJ where 1 tonne-m \approx 9.81 kJ)
Eq 4-3: E_{area} = \frac{N_{drops} \cdot W \cdot H \cdot g}{A_{grid}}, energy per unit area (kJ/m^2) where N_{drops} is number of drops per print and A_{grid} is grid area per print
Eq 4-4: D_{effective} \approx (2/3 \text{ to } 3/4) \cdot D, effective depth of significant improvement

sections.title: DDC Design
sections.summary: DDC design selects tamper weight, drop height, grid spacing, number of drops per print, number of passes, and time between passes. Process: (1) estimate depth using D = n×sqrt(W×H); (2) select W and H; (3) design grid spacing (typically 1.5-2.0 × D_max); (4) specify number of drops per print (stop when crater depth <0.2 m per blow or surface heave occurs); (5) apply ironing pass for upper 1-2 m.
sections.body: DDC design involves selecting the tamper weight, drop height, grid spacing, number of drops per print, number of passes, and time between passes to achieve the target improvement over the required depth and area. The design process begins with estimating the required depth of influence using D = n*sqrt(W*H) and selecting W and H to achieve this depth with available equipment. The grid spacing for the primary (deep) pass is typically 1.5 to 2.5 times the depth of influence D. The number of drops per print is determined by the required energy per unit area, typically 5-15 drops for the primary pass. A rest period of 1-4 weeks between passes allows excess pore water pressures to dissipate in partially saturated or silty soils. The ironing pass uses lower energy (lighter weight, lower drop height) on a closer grid spacing (1.5-3 m) to densify the upper 2-3 m that is loosened by the primary impacts. Post-improvement verification typically requires SPT, CPT, or pressuremeter testing at selected locations to confirm that the target soil properties have been achieved. A test section of 3-5 print locations is recommended before full-scale production to calibrate the design parameters.
key_points: Design selects tamper weight, drop height, grid spacing, drops per print, passes, and rest period
Deep pass grid spacing typically 1.5-2.5 times the depth of influence D
Number of drops per print: typically 5-15 for primary pass based on energy per unit area
Rest period of 1-4 weeks between passes for pore pressure dissipation in silty soils
Ironing pass: lower energy, closer grid (1.5-3 m), densifies upper 2-3 m
Post-improvement verification: SPT, CPT, or pressuremeter testing
Test section of 3-5 prints recommended before full-scale production
equations: S_{grid} = (1.5 \text{ to } 2.5) \cdot D, primary pass grid spacing
N_{drops} = \frac{E_{area} \cdot A_{grid}}{W \cdot H \cdot g}, number of drops per print to achieve target energy per unit area

sections.title: Vibro-Compaction - Description
sections.summary: Vibro-compaction (vibroflotation) densifies granular soils by inserting a 300-500 mm diameter vibrating probe (vibroflot) and using horizontal vibrations to rearrange soil particles into a denser state. The vibroflot generates centrifugal force of 150-400 kN at 20-60 Hz, causing liquefaction and densification around the probe. Backfill (coarse sand or gravel) is added from the surface as the vibroflot withdraws.
sections.body: Vibro-compaction (also called vibroflotation) densifies loose granular soils by inserting a vibrating probe (vibroflot) into the ground and using horizontal vibrations to rearrange soil particles into a denser state. The vibroflot is a cylindrical probe 300-500 mm in diameter and 2-4 m long, containing an eccentric rotating weight that generates horizontal vibrations at the probe tip with centrifugal forces of 150-500 kN and frequencies of 25-60 Hz. The probe is lowered into the ground using water jetting or vibration to the target depth, then slowly withdrawn while vibrating. As the soil densifies, the ground surface settles and granular backfill material is added to compensate for volume reduction, typically 5-15% of the treated volume. Vibro-compaction can treat granular soils to depths of 15-20 m and occasionally deeper. The process is clean, produces minimal spoil, and has lower vibration impacts on surrounding structures compared to DDC. Vibro-compaction was developed in Germany in the 1930s and has been used on thousands of projects worldwide.
key_points: Densifies loose granular soils using a vibrating probe (vibroflot) that generates horizontal vibrations
Vibroflot: 300-500 mm diameter, 2-4 m long, eccentric weight generating 150-500 kN centrifugal force at 25-60 Hz
Probe lowered to target depth using water jetting, then slowly withdrawn while vibrating
Backfill added to compensate for 5-15% volume reduction as soil densifies
Treatment depth up to 15-20 m or deeper
Lower vibration impact on surrounding structures compared to DDC
Developed in Germany in the 1930s; thousands of worldwide applications

sections.title: Vibro-Compaction Suitability Number
sections.summary: Brown (1977) suitability number SN quantifies treatability from grain size: SN = 1.7 × sqrt(3/(D50)² + 1/(D20)² + 1/(D10)²), where D50, D20, D10 are particle diameters in mm. SN < 10: excellent; 10-20: good; 20-30: fair; 30-50: poor; >50: unsuitable. Soil with high fines content (>15%) produces high SN values and is generally unsuitable for vibro-compaction without modification.
sections.body: The effectiveness of vibro-compaction is strongly dependent on the grain size distribution of the soil being treated. Brown (1977) developed the suitability number SN to quantify the treatability of a soil based on its grain size distribution. The suitability number is calculated as SN = 1.7 * sqrt(3/(D50)^2 + 1/(D20)^2 + 1/(D10)^2), where D50, D20, and D10 are the particle diameters in mm at which 50%, 20%, and 10% of the soil is finer by weight. Soils with SN < 10 are classified as excellent candidates for vibro-compaction, SN = 10-20 as good, SN = 20-30 as fair, SN = 30-50 as poor, and SN > 50 as unsuitable. The suitability number increases (decreasing treatability) with decreasing grain size and increasing fines content. As a general guideline, vibro-compaction is effective when the fines content (passing No. 200 sieve) is less than 12-15% and the clay content is less than 2-3%. Soils with higher fines content may require vibro-replacement (stone columns) instead, where the probe displacement is backfilled with coarse aggregate to create composite stone column elements.
key_points: Brown (1977) suitability number SN quantifies vibro-compaction treatability from grain size distribution
SN < 10: excellent; SN 10-20: good; SN 20-30: fair; SN 30-50: poor; SN > 50: unsuitable
SN increases (less suitable) with decreasing grain size and increasing fines content
General guideline: effective when fines content < 12-15% and clay content < 2-3%
Soils with higher fines content may require vibro-replacement (stone columns) instead
D50, D20, D10 are particle diameters (mm) at 50%, 20%, 10% finer by weight

sections.title: Vibro-Compaction Probe Spacing and Design
sections.summary: Probe spacing (1.5-4.0 m, triangular preferred) is the primary design variable. Effective treatment radius per probe is typically 1.0-2.5 m. Design targets post-treatment relative density Dr ≥ 70-80% for liquefaction mitigation, or minimum SPT N60 or CPT qc values. QC uses CPT or SPT before/after treatment; post-treatment verification typically 24-72 hours after installation.
sections.body: Vibro-compaction probe spacing is the primary design variable controlling the degree of densification. Closer probe spacing results in greater energy input per unit volume and higher post-treatment relative density. Typical probe spacings range from 1.5 to 4.0 m in triangular or square patterns, with triangular patterns preferred for uniform treatment. The effective treatment radius of a single probe depends on the vibroflot power, soil grain size, initial relative density, and target relative density. For typical vibroflots (150-300 kN centrifugal force), the effective radius is approximately 1.5-3.0 m. Design proceeds by selecting a target relative density (typically Dr = 60-80% for bearing capacity or liquefaction mitigation), estimating the required energy per unit volume based on empirical correlations, and computing the probe spacing. Post-improvement verification using SPT or CPT at the centroid of the probe pattern (worst case location) is required to confirm that target densities are achieved. The total volume change from densification is typically 5-15% of the treated volume, requiring backfill. Design must also consider the depth of loose surface material that is not improved by the vibroflot and may require surface compaction or a compacted fill cap.
key_points: Probe spacing is the primary design variable: closer spacing = greater densification

Target relative density typically Dr = 60-80% for bearing capacity or liquefaction mitigation
Post-improvement verification at centroid of probe pattern (worst case location)
Volume change from densification: 5-15% of treated volume, requiring backfill
Loose surface material (top 1-2 m) not improved by vibroflot; requires separate treatment

sections.title: Case Histories
sections.summary: DDC case: Trident submarine base (Kings Bay, GA, 1981-1984) treated 500,000 m² of loose hydraulic fill to 7-12 m depth using 15-33 t tampers from 12-30 m, achieving target SPT N > 15 blows/ft. Vibro-compaction case: I-90 interchange (Seattle) treated loose sand fills to 10-12 m depth at 2.5 m triangular spacing, increasing CPT qc from 3-5 MPa to >15 MPa.
sections.body: Deep dynamic compaction and vibro-compaction have been used on hundreds of transportation projects in the United States and worldwide. The DDC treatment of the Trident submarine base in Kings Bay, Georgia (1981-1984) is one of the largest DDC projects ever performed, treating over 500,000 m^2 of loose hydraulic fill to depths of 7-12 m using 15-33 tonne tampers dropped from 12-30 m heights, achieving SPT N-values of 15-25 from initial values of 3-8. The Newark Airport North Terminal redevelopment (2000) used DDC to densify loose sand fills and hydraulic fill to depths of 6-8 m, reducing liquefaction potential and supporting new terminal structures. Vibro-compaction was used at the Palm Jumeirah in Dubai to densify hydraulically placed sand fill for the artificial island construction, treating millions of cubic meters with probe spacings of 2.5-3.5 m to achieve relative densities exceeding 60%. In the US, vibro-compaction has been used extensively for liquefaction mitigation at bridge sites in seismically active regions including California, Washington, and South Carolina. These case histories confirm that deep compaction technologies reliably achieve target densification when soil conditions are within the applicability range and adequate quality control is maintained.
key_points: Kings Bay, GA (1981-1984): 500,000+ m^2 DDC of loose hydraulic fill, SPT N improved from 3-8 to 15-25
Newark Airport (2000): DDC of loose sand/hydraulic fill to 6-8 m depth for liquefaction mitigation
Palm Jumeirah, Dubai: vibro-compaction of millions of m^3 hydraulic sand fill to Dr > 60%
US vibro-compaction for liquefaction mitigation at bridge sites in CA, WA, SC

Adequate quality control (SPT/CPT verification) is essential for confirming improvement
